cur:catacombs-maius-virgin-child-orans.summary: In an arcosolium lunette a veiled woman with large eyes raises her hands in prayer, a child placed before her breast, between two chi-rho monograms. The painting has long been celebrated as one of the earliest images of the Virgin Mary with the Christ Child in prayer, a forerunner of the later 'Virgin of the Sign'.
facts: The chi-rho monograms – the first letters of Christ's name in Greek – flank the figure on both sides.
Commons classifies the image among 4th-century paintings of the Madonna and Child and among images of the 'Theotokos of the Sign' type.
cur:catacombs-maius-virgin-child-orans.notes: Many scholars think the woman may be the deceased with her child rather than the Virgin and Christ; the identification remains uncertain.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-61-christ.summary: The psalmist raises one hand to the heavens, where the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos stands among angels with spear and shield as his 'rock and salvation', and with the other points to sinners below, some killing each other, others cheating at the scales. Pieces of a 'bowing wall' and 'tottering fence' lie at his feet. The lower drawing of folio 34v shows the soul that 'waiteth upon God' amid a deceitful world.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-61-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:objects3-breamore-rood.summary: Over the doorway in the porch of the Anglo-Saxon church at Breamore, a large stone rood shows Christ on the cross between the Virgin Mary and St John, beneath the hand of God reaching down from a cloud. The figures were cut back flush with the wall, probably at the Reformation, so that what survives is chiefly their outline and traces of medieval painting around them; even so the composition of the Cross between the two mourners is still plain.
facts: St Mary's, Breamore, is an almost complete Anglo-Saxon church; an Old English inscription of the reign of Æthelred the Unready survives on the arch to its south porticus.
The roundel of the Lamb of God set below the rood is a later, 12th-century addition.
cur:objects3-breamore-rood.notes: Badly mutilated; the date is approximate and usually given as around 1000. The Reformation as the occasion of the defacement is the usual explanation, not a documented fact.

Q26781788.summary: On a sunlit slope before the Temple in Jerusalem, an angry crowd drags a woman accused of adultery toward Christ, who sits calmly among his disciples. Polenov paints the moment just before Christ's famous answer, turning the story into a vast, light-filled scene of the Holy Land. More than three metres high and six wide, it was the fruit of nearly two decades of work and travel.
facts: Polenov travelled to Egypt, Palestine and Syria in 1881–82 and later worked in Rome in 1883–84, gathering studies of landscape, architecture and people for the painting.
The censor would not allow Polenov's intended title, 'Who Is Without Sin?', in the catalogue, and it was exhibited as 'Christ and the Sinner' (Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery).

It was bought by Tsar Alexander III at the Peredvizhniki exhibition of 1887 and hung in the Winter Palace before passing to the newly founded Russian Museum in 1897; Polenov then re-dated the canvas 1888.
